title: Rep. Chuck Edwards withdraws from re-election after ethics censure recommendation
dek: Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) announced August 5, 2026 that he is withdrawing from his re-election campaign days after the House Ethics Committee recommended censure over allegations of inappropriate conduct toward two female staffers. The committee found no evidence of sexual activity or quid pro quo harassment but concluded Edwards engaged in unprofessional behavior including lavish gifts, appearance comments, and invitations to intimate dinners.
author: The GoCheckMyNews Desk
key_fact: Edwards withdrew from re-election on August 5, 2026, two days after the bipartisan House Ethics Committee recommended censure for conduct toward staff that the panel found would lead a reasonable observer to interpret as sexual or romantic harassment.
bottom_line: Congressional member withdraws from race following ethics censure recommendation; widely corroborated across spectrum affecting 2026 midterms landscape.
body: Rep. Chuck Edwards announced early Wednesday, August 5, 2026 that he is withdrawing from his re-election campaign, two days after the House Ethics Committee recommended censure over allegations that he engaged in unprofessional and inappropriate conduct toward two female staffers.

The North Carolina Republican, 65, issued a brief statement: "After much prayer and reflection, I've decided to withdraw from my re-election campaign. I will complete my current term. Serving Western North Carolina has been the honor of my life. Thank you for your trust, prayers, and support."

On Monday, August 3, the bipartisan Ethics Committee released a 25-page report recommending censure after finding that Edwards "violated the House Code of Official Conduct by failing to adhere to the spirit of rules prohibiting sexual harassment of and unwanted advances to House staffers." The committee concluded Edwards engaged in "persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct" including providing "lavish and recurrent gifts, making comments regarding their appearance and dress, inviting them to intimate dinners and vacations, sending notes regarding his effusive affection, and inviting them to other activities as a way to spend time together." The committee stated this pattern of behavior "would lead a reasonable observer to interpret it as" sexual or romantic harassment.

The committee's findings stopped short of the most serious allegations. The panel found no evidence that Edwards engaged in sexual activity with or propositioned any staffers, and it concluded the allegations "do not implicate quid pro quo sexual harassment" or violate "the 'letter' of federal sexual harassment law."

Edwards has denied that his conduct was intended to be sexual or romantic in nature. His counsel submitted a 15-page rebuttal to the committee's findings, calling them "unfounded," and Edwards cooperated with the investigation. In May, when the allegations first surfaced, Edwards told NBC News he welcomed an investigation and called the allegations "baseless."

Edwards, a former state lawmaker, ousted Rep. Madison Cawthorn in the 2022 GOP primary. His withdrawal from the race removes a sitting congressman from the 2026 midterm battlefield in a competitive Western North Carolina district. The House has not yet voted on the censure recommendation; the timeline and procedures for that vote remain unclear.

The Bottom Line: Edwards' departure from the race tests whether ethics committee findings carry sufficient institutional weight to force members from office even without criminal charges. Watch whether the full House votes on the censure recommendation and whether other members facing ethical scrutiny cite this outcome in their own calculations.
